newsitem.title: USA: New Jersey jury sentences Megan's killer to death.
newsitem.headline: New Jersey jury sentences Megan's killer to death.

text.p: A New Jersey jury Friday sentenced a convicted child molester to death for raping and strangling 7-year-old Megan Kanka, whose murder nearly three years ago inspired so-called Megan's Laws around the nation.
The jury in Mercer County deliberated for 10 hours over two days before deciding Jesse Timmendequas, 36, should be executed for the 1994 murder. The same jury convicted him on May 30.
Timmendequas, who looked down at the table before him as the sentence was read, had no visible response as the jury forewoman read the decision.
Megan's mother Maureen Kanka sobbed on her husband Richard's shoulder.
Superior Court Judge Andrew Smithson set an execution date of Aug. 1, but under New Jersey law Timmendequas is entitled to an automatic appeal.
Timmendequas had agreed to waive any possibility of parole if the jury decided he should not be executed.

After the verdict, Smithson praised the parents, saying, "Maureen and Richard Kanka have endured a loss that is truly impossible to imagine. They buried their child. They had to wait for three years until justice was meted out to Megan."

The Kankas and their supporters gathered outside the courthouse afterward. Richard Kanka, his arm around his wife, told reporters: "We asked the prosecutor's office to go for the maximum (penalty) and we never wavered from that initial thought."
"He will never, ever, ever get out to harm another little girl," Maureen Kanka said. The sentence "gave Megan's life some value."

The defence had offered the jury 25 mitigating factors to weigh, including that he had been under severe emotional stress, that he was not aware that his actions were wrong and that his childhood was filled with sexual abuse that made him mentally ill.

While the jury agreed that some of the mitigating factors offered were valid, and said it was possible he may have been abused as a child, it did not outweigh their belief that Timmendequas killed Megan to avoid being caught for raping her, and that he murdered her in the course of raping and kidnapping her.

Trial testimony showed that Timmendequas lured the girl into his home in suburban Hamilton Township, New Jersey, where he attacked her. The Kanka family did not know he was a twice-convicted child molester when he moved into their neighbourhood.

The attack became the inspiration for Megan's Laws around the country that require child molesters to register with police, and in 1996, President Clinton signed a federal law making it easier to get information about released sex offenders.
